en: The Mahāvaipulya Ratnakoṭa Sūtra, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada.
In a vihāra, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus and five thousand bodhisattvas,
the World-Honored One was then staying at the site of the Karīra-flower grove, surrounded by a great multitude of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas as he expounded the Dharma.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī, surrounded by five hundred bodhisattvas, Śakras, Brahmās, and world-protectors who paid him respectful homage, proceeded to where the World-Honored One was.
Having arrived, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times, and withdrew to sit to one side;
the bodhisattvas and their retinue likewise sat to one side.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"What Dharma has the Tathāgata taught today?
Continue to explain it in succession so that it is not interrupted.
Then, the Venerable Subhūti said to Mañjuśrī:
“The World-Honored One has previously taught the Dharma for the śrāvakas. Mañjuśrī!
I now request you to teach the Dharma for bodhisattvas.”
Then the youth Mañjuśrī said to Subhūti,
"Venerable One!
Of what use are the dharmas of a bodhisattva now?"
"Venerable Subhūti!
All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are not vessels for the Dharma of a bodhisattva. Subhūti said:
"Mañjuśrī! We pray that you will expound [this teaching]; sentient beings who are fit vessels shall naturally listen and receive it.
The youth Mañjuśrī replied:
“Venerable Subhūti!
Are you now able to know who is a vessel for this Buddha-dharma and who is not?
Subhūti replied:
“Mañjuśrī! We śrāvakas understand through the voices of others; how could we possibly know who is a vessel for the Buddha’s Dharma and who is not? Mañjuśrī!”
"I request that you declare who among us is a vessel for the Buddha's Dharma and who is not.
Mañjuśrī replied, "Venerable Subhūti!..."
All those who have entered the stage of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*) are not suitable vessels, for they are already bound and sustained by the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

However, those who contemplate the dharma-realm yet do not abandon or forsake any sentient beings, who do not fall into the stage of certainty and do not dwell together with the fetters (*saṃyojana*), such persons are vessels for the Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti!

If one who has reached the realm of the dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is bound by it, abandoning all sentient beings who are scorched by their fetters, and with a mind weary and terrified of the triple world, not delighting in dwelling within fetters for even a single thought-moment—such persons are called those who are not vessels for the Buddha-dharma.
"Venerable Subhūti!

If there are those who, throughout all kalpas until the end of the future, give rise to great adornment without fear or dread; who practice within the three realms without being defiled by the three impurities; who conceive of birth and death as a pleasure garden; and who, though desiring the various realms of existence, do not accumulate the formations that lead to existence—such persons are called vessels for the Buddha-dharma."
Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti! If one manifests desire and defilement while being free from desire and defilement;

manifests anger while being free from malice; manifests delusion while being free from the obscuration of ignorance; and though having severed the fetters and proclivities, manifests dwelling within the three realms; guides sentient beings without any self-exaltation; bears the heavy burden of all sentient beings; and is able to ensure that the lineage of the unsurpassed Triple Gem remains complete and unbroken while abiding in the gate of samādhi—persons such as these are called vessels for the Buddha-dharma.
The Venerable Subhūti said to Mañjuśrī:
"The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is one, suchness, and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi); how can you distinguish between those who are vessels and those who are not?"
Mañjuśrī said: "Venerable Subhūti!

It is like a potter who fashions various kinds of vessels from a single kind of clay; though they are all fired by one fire—some becoming vessels for oil, some for ghee, some for honey, or some for impurities—the nature of that clay remains without distinction, and the burning of the fire likewise remains without distinction."
"So it is, so it is, Venerable Subhūti!
Within the single dharma-nature, the single suchness, and the single reality-limit, there are distinctions among the vessels according to their karmic conduct:
the vessel of ghee and oil is a metaphor for the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; that honey vessel is a metaphor for the bodhisattvas; and the impure vessel is a metaphor for ordinary worldlings."
Subhūti said: "Mañjuśrī!
Is there such a vessel that is called a non-vessel, yet a non-vessel is [actually] a vessel?"
Mañjuśrī said, "There is. Subhūti said:
"What is it? Mañjuśrī replied, "Venerable Subhūti!..."
All fetters and afflictions are called "unfit vessels"; all habitual tendencies of the fetters are called "unfit vessels.
These are called unfit vessels, yet they are also said to be the vessels for the Buddha-dharma.
"If one has severed all afflictions, such a person is not a vessel for the Buddha's Dharma.
Subhūti asked: "As for what you call a 'vessel,' what is it intended to contain?"
Mañjuśrī said: "To have no contents is to be full.
If that which is contained does not leak, one knows it to be an intact vessel."
If what is contained within leaks away, one knows it is a broken vessel.
Venerable Subhūti!
Just as space is the vessel for all medicinal herbs, trees, and forests, yet it is not a vessel.
In this way, Venerable Subhūti, it is likewise with the bodhisattva:
he is a vessel for the Buddha-dharma, yet he is not a vessel.
Venerable Subhūti!
Just as all trees born from the earth grow by means of empty space as their vessel,
so too, Venerable Subhūti,
the bodhisattva is born from various wholesome minds and grows by means of the vessel that is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Subhūti asked: "In what way, then, does this bodhisattva increase?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"As space increases, so too does the bodhisattva increase; yet this bodhisattva neither increases nor diminishes. Why is this? "
"One neither increases the fetters and afflictions nor regresses from the Buddha-dharma. Subhūti said: "Mañjuśrī!"
"What is the difference between the Buddha-dharma and the fetters?
Mañjuśrī replied, "Venerable Subhūti!..."
Just as wherever the light of Sumeru, the king of mountains, shines, all things become of one color—
namely, the color of gold; so too, Subhūti,
wherever the light of prajñā shines, all fetters (saṃyojana) become of one color, namely, the color of the Buddha-dharma.
Therefore, Subhūti!
When the dharmas of the Buddha and the fetters are observed with the wisdom of prajñā, they are equal and without distinction.
For this reason, Venerable Subhūti!
"All dharmas are the Buddha-dharma. Subhūti said: "Mañjuśrī!"
"For what reason are all phenomena (dharmas) the Buddha-dharma?
Mañjuśrī replied,
"Because they are realized by the wisdom of the Buddha."
He asked again:
"In what way is it as awakened by the Buddha's wisdom?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"Just as it was at the beginning, so it is at the end; because it does not depart from suchness (tathatā), it is therefore said that 'it is realized by the wisdom of a Buddha.
He asked again:
"Regarding what you say about the beginning and the end, what constitutes the beginning and the end?"
Mañjuśrī replied:
"Because it is empty at the beginning and quiescent at the end, it is called 'beginning and end. Subhūti said:
“What is the difference between emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and tranquility (*śānti*)?
Mañjuśrī replied, “Venerable Subhūti!...”
"What do you think?
What difference is there between raw gold and refined gold?
He replied:
"It is by means of verbal expression that there is distinction.
Mañjuśrī said, "So it is, Venerable Subhūti!"
"It is by means of verbal expression that one speaks of 'emptiness' and 'quiescence.
If there is a wise person, they do not cling to words nor grasp at words. Subhūti said:
“Mañjuśrī! What is the distinguishing characteristic between ordinary beings and the wise? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Venerable Subhūti!
As the Buddha has taught, it is by virtue of the characteristics of karma that one is called an ordinary person, and it is by virtue of the characteristics of karma that one is called a wise person.”
Subhūti said: “Mañjuśrī, what are the characteristics of karma?”

Mañjuśrī said: "Conditioned causes and conditions constitute its characteristic; according to what one practices, there are distinct names. If there is nothing practiced, then there are no distinct names."

Ordinary persons have practice and have names for distinctions; the wise have no practice and no names for distinctions; that which lies between existence and non-existence is called the noble practice.
Yet this noble practice is called "non-practice" to ordinary persons.
He asked again:
"Mañjuśrī! What is meant by the term 'noble one' (ārya)?"
Mañjuśrī replied,
“Because we have equally entered the state of non-attachment and non-contention.
He asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! Are there any dharmas that also enter the phrase of non-attachment and non-contention?
Mañjuśrī replied:
“There is, Venerable Subhūti! Subhūti said:
“What is it? He replied, “Subhūti!...”
Just as all rivers, once they have entered the great ocean,
become of one salty taste; so too, Subhūti,
all dharmas enter into non-attachment and non-contention and become of one single taste, namely, the taste of liberation.
Subhūti said: "By being liberated from what is it called 'liberation'?
Mañjuśrī replied:
“Venerable Subhūti!
By what causes and conditions is there one who is bound, or one who is unbound?
Subhūti replied:
“Because of ignorance, there is bondage.
Mañjuśrī said, “It is so;
because ignorance is severed, it is called liberation.”
Subhūti said: "Since all phenomena are equal, how can one speak of wisdom and the absence of wisdom?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"Just as water in the heat of spring is called 'hot water,' and water when cold falls in winter is called 'cold water,' yet there is no difference in the nature of the water itself;
so it is, Subhūti!"
That which is scorched by the afflictions of improper reflection is called "ignorance," whereas that which involves proper reflection is called "wisdom.
However, within this context, there is no person (pudgala) who is designated as either wise or ignorant.
Subhūti said: "Mañjuśrī! This meaning is difficult to realize."
Mañjuśrī said: "Venerable Subhūti, it is because they practice dualistic conduct."
Subhūti said: “This meaning is difficult to perceive. Mañjuśrī said:
"Because they lack the eye of wisdom.
Subhūti said, "This meaning is difficult to enter."
Mañjuśrī said: "Because its bottom cannot be reached. Subhūti said:
"This meaning is difficult to understand.
Mañjuśrī replied, "Because of overweening pride."
Subhūti said: “This meaning is difficult to realize. Mañjuśrī said:
"Because of the abandonment of discursive thought. Subhūti said:
"This meaning is difficult to escape from."
Mañjuśrī said: “Because they delight in their nests and caves. Subhūti said:
"This meaning is difficult to conceive. Mañjuśrī said:
"Because within it there is the practice of signlessness. Subhūti said:
"This meaning is difficult to awaken to and difficult to contemplate.
Mañjuśrī said, "Because within it there is no verbal expression."
Subhūti said: "This meaning cannot be apprehended. Mañjuśrī said:
"Because within this there is not even the slightest meaning.
Subhūti said: "This meaning is that which is understood by the wise."
Mañjuśrī replied, “Because one understands the nature of one’s own mind. [The Buddha said,] “Mañjuśrī!”
“The Tathāgata has spoken of what is beneficial and what is not beneficial.
For what reason, World-Honored One, did you speak these words? Mañjuśrī said:
“Venerable Subhūti!
That which is called ‘benefit’ is termed ‘unobtainable.
To desire to obtain anything within this matter is for that benefit to be termed ‘non-benefit.’”
"Venerable Subhūti!
Furthermore, that which is beneficial is called 'quiescence.
If, within this, one gives rise to the activities of body and mind, then that benefit is called 'non-benefit.'"
"Therefore, the Tathāgata says that benefit is not benefit. Subhūti said:
"As the Buddha has taught, all dharmas are non-dharmas."
"What does this mean? Mañjuśrī replied,
"Venerable Subhūti!"
As the Buddha has taught: "Those who understand my Dharma as being like the parable of the raft should abandon even the Dharma, let alone that which is not the Dharma.
If the Dharma is to be abandoned, it is no longer called "Dharma," nor is it called "non-Dharma."
Subhūti said: “Mañjuśrī! Can the Buddha-dharma of the Tathāgata be non-Dharma?”
Mañjuśrī said: "Venerable Subhūti!

The Buddha-dharma of the Tathāgata is without fixed determination. If there is no fixed determination, then one should not speak of this as 'dharma' or 'non-dharma. Therefore, the Buddha says that all dharmas are non-dharmas."
Subhūti said: “It is rare, Mañjuśrī!
That a bodhisattva who has newly set out in the practice would hear such a teaching and not be struck with fear.”
Mañjuśrī said: "What do you think?
When Prince Siṃha hears the lion's roar, does he feel any fear or alarm?"
“Suppose a young goose were traveling through the sky;
would it fear falling from the air? Subhūti replied, “No.”
"Mañjuśrī! Mañjuśrī replied, "So it is, Subhūti!"

If there is a bodhisattva of the Tathāgata lineage who has gone to the suchness (tathatā) and is born from suchness, they will hear all dharmas, all sounds, and all that is spoken without being startled or afraid.
"Venerable Subhūti!
For one who possesses fear, what is it that they fear?
Subhūti replied:
“If one regards the view of a self as truly existent, then there will be fear.
Mañjuśrī said: “Because a bodhisattva understands and realizes the view of a self, they do not give rise to alarm or fear toward any phenomena, any sounds, or anything that is spoken.”
Subhūti said: "Mañjuśrī!
If a bodhisattva understands and comprehends the view of self, why do they not attain the fruit?"
Mañjuśrī said: "There is no bodhisattva who attains the realization of a fruit.
A bodhisattva merely observes and knows; they do not grasp at the realization of a fruit, but proceed toward the wisdom of a Buddha."
“A bodhisattva constantly cultivates great compassion toward all sentient beings; although they understand the view of a self, they do not fall into the realization of [personal] fruits.
Subhūti asked: “Does this bodhisattva possess skillful means such that, although they understand the view of a self, they do not grasp at the fruit?”
Mañjuśrī said: “It is so, Venerable One!
If there is a bodhisattva who is embraced by the realm of wisdom and skillful means, that bodhisattva, although aware of the view of self, does not grasp at its fruit.”
"Venerable Subhūti!
It is as when a strong man grasps a sharp sword and cuts down a śāla tree; although it is severed, it remains standing and does not immediately fall.
In this same way, Subhūti!"
If a bodhisattva possesses great compassion and great wisdom of skillful means toward all sentient beings, although they know the view of a self, they do not realize the fruit [of arhatship].
O Venerable Subhūti!
At times, when the heavens send down a great and copious rain, these śāla trees immediately sprout again; they produce leaves, flowers, and fruits to benefit sentient beings.
In this same way, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva is thoroughly moistened by great loving-kindness and great compassion, the bodhisattva’s realm of wisdom returns to arise within the triple world, manifesting the acceptance of birth and death according to their spiritual lineage to bring great benefit to all sentient beings.
"Venerable Subhūti!
Suppose a great wind blows upon these śāla trees, and their branches, twigs, stems, and fruits fall to the ground.
In this same way, Venerable Subhūti!"
"These bodhisattvas, blown by the fierce winds of great wisdom, fall upon the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and are ultimately and forever extinguished.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Mañjuśrī:
"Excellent, excellent!"
He skillfully expounds the realm of the bodhisattva’s wisdom and skillful means, preaching the Dharma in conjunction with great loving-kindness and great compassion. Mañjuśrī,
listen as I speak a parable.

Just as when a great dragon king conceives such a thought, he raises a vast cloud that pervades the sky; from within that cloud, he rains down hot thunderbolts that burn everything they reach, yet he also rains down great torrents of water for the sake of growth.

In this way, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva of skillful means raises the clouds of great wisdom and skillful means; they manifest and engage in all the activities of ordinary worldlings to teach and transform them, while manifesting and engaging in the conduct of the noble ones to subdue sentient beings.

“Mañjuśrī! Just as a great fragrant tree has a root fragrance that differs from the fragrance of its trunk, the fragrance of its leaves, the fragrance of its flowers, and the fragrance of its fruits—each being distinct and different.”

In this way, Mañjuśrī, it is also with the fragrant body of wisdom possessed by a bodhisattva: according to what various sentient beings should hear and understand, it emits the corresponding fragrance of the Dharma; yet, while its root of great compassion blazes forth, it remains unmoved.

“Mañjuśrī! It is like the Vaiḍūrya maṇi jewel on the neck of Śakra, which universally and completely illuminates the Heaven of the Thirty-three; by the power of that jewel, all things therein are made manifest.
Yet this jewel has no conceptualization.”
In this way, Mañjuśrī!
A pure precious gem is a metaphor for the bodhisattva’s cognitive nature manifesting all phenomena, yet that bodhisattva has no conceptualization whatsoever regarding them.
“Mañjuśrī! Just as a wish-fulfilling jewel can fulfill all the wishes of sentient beings, yet that precious gem has no thoughts or perceptions;

so it is, Mañjuśrī, with the precious jewel of a bodhisattva’s pure mind, which can fulfill all the wishes of sentient beings, while remaining free from thoughts and perceptions in all circumstances.”
“Mañjuśrī! Just as fire blazes because of space and rain falls because of space, yet this space has neither cold nor heat; so it is, Mañjuśrī!”

The Bodhisattva of Skillful Means dwells within the triple world yet practices the tranquility of nirvana without being afflicted by the fever of the fetters; remaining unstained and unattached amidst the Buddha-dharma, he brings benefit to both.
“Mañjuśrī! Just as from space both poisonous trees and medicinal trees grow, yet that space is neither harmed by the poison nor purified by the medicine.”
Thus it is, Mañjuśrī!

If there is a bodhisattva possessing wisdom and skillful means, the body of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is like a poisonous tree, while the five faculties such as faith (*pañcendriya*) are like medicinal trees; neither are they defiled by the fetters of the aggregates, nor are they purified by the fetters of the faculties, for both possess utility.
“Mañjuśrī! It is like a water-strainer: if it is briefly blocked, the water does not leak; yet if it is briefly opened, the water leaks.
In the same way, Mañjuśrī!”

If there is a bodhisattva possessing wisdom and skillful means who dwells in samādhi, accomplishing great penetration without attachment to any realm, and who, upon briefly arising from concentration, manifests within the various realms of outflows, he expounds the Dharma according to what is appropriate for each being.
“Mañjuśrī! Just as a fine bird that well protects its downy plumage does not spare its own body, so it is, Mañjuśrī!”
The Bodhisattva who abides in great compassion skillfully protects sentient beings without cherishing his own body. "Mañjuśrī!
Just as the lion, king of beasts, has nothing to fear except for a raging fire."
In this way, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva who employs skillful means does not fear anything, with the sole exception of the liberation of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. “Mañjuśrī!
Just as the elephant-king Airāvaṇa, though belonging to the realm of animals, is able to manifest all manner of magnificent ornaments through the power of Śakra’s merit, so it is, Mañjuśrī!
Bodhisattvas are thus able to manifest the adornments of the Dharma even within the animal realm, transforming and liberating beings according to their needs. "Mañjuśrī!
It is like fire produced from a fire-drill and fire produced from a precious gem; both are capable of burning."
In this way, Mañjuśrī!

Whether it be a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind or one at the final moment of mind at the site of enlightenment, both are able to burn away all the fetters and afflictions of all sentient beings.
“Mañjuśrī! Just as various trees possess diverse colors, diverse fragrances, and diverse fruits, all of which grow and develop by means of the four great elements.”
In this way, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva gathers all roots of goodness through various gateways; all of these are subsumed within the bodhicitta and dedicated toward awakening for the sake of its growth.
“Mañjuśrī! Just as when the wheel-treasure of a universal monarch moves forward, the fourfold army follows it; so too, Mañjuśrī!”
“Mañjuśrī, wherever the Bodhisattva’s perfection of the wisdom of skillful means goes, all the factors conducive to enlightenment follow after it.”
"Just as the chick within the egg of the king of birds, the kalaviṅka, utters the exquisite song of the kalaviṅka even before its beak has appeared, so it is, Mañjuśrī!"

The bodhisattvas within the egg of the Buddha-dharma have not yet destroyed the view of self and have not yet emerged from the triple world; nevertheless, they are able to produce the wondrous sounds of the Buddha-dharma, namely the sounds of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
“Mañjuśrī! Just as a kalaviṅka bird, having entered among a flock of peacocks, never utters its cry, but only resumes its cry once it returns to the midst of the kalaviṅka birds;”
In this way, Mañjuśrī!

If a bodhisattva enters among the assembly of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they shall never expound the inconceivable Dharma of the Buddhas; it is only when they reach the assembly of bodhisattvas that they then expound it.
“Mañjuśrī! Just as the great whirlwind cannot be resisted by any trees or mountains within the realm of Jambudvīpa, so it is, Mañjuśrī!”

When a Bodhisattva expounds the inconceivable teachings of the Buddhas, the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—whether those in training (śaikṣa) or those beyond training (aśaikṣa)—are unable to believe or understand them unless they are sustained by the Buddha’s protection; if they do believe and understand, it is because they are sustained by the Buddha’s protection.
“Mañjuśrī! It is just as the light emitted from the solar palace shines equally upon both the pure and the defiled, without increase or decrease, and there is no one who can criticize it.”
In this way, Mañjuśrī!

A bodhisattva who employs skillful means emits the radiance of wisdom; though it is shared with all ordinary beings, it is not destroyed by them, and though it is shared with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, it is not defiled by them. No one is able to revile the light of a bodhisattva’s skillful means and wisdom.
“Mañjuśrī! Just as when the leaves of the pārijātaka-kovidāra tree fall, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven rejoice and leap for joy, saying:
‘Before long, this tree shall produce flowers and fruit.’”
"In this way, Mañjuśrī!

If there is a bodhisattva who is able to renounce everything, at that time all Buddhas will be greatly rejoiced, and before long this bodhisattva shall, together with all sentient beings, give birth to the fruit of the Dharma of the Lotus Sūtra."
“Mañjuśrī! Just as a supple tree moves and sways with the wind without fear of being broken, so it is, Mañjuśrī!”
A bodhisattva who is well able to accord with sentient beings does not fear falling into the stages of all śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
"Mañjuśrī! It is just as water flows downward in accordance with its course."
In this way, Mañjuśrī!
The bodhisattva free from pride is also like this, flowing toward and inclining toward all-knowledge.
"Mañjuśrī! [he said].
It is just as when the great ocean first settles, its location is the lowest of all, and only then do all the streams flow into it.
In this same way, Mañjuśrī!
When Bodhisattvas eliminate pride and arrogance, the Buddha-dharma will then flow entirely toward them. "Mañjuśrī!
It is like a vajra jewel, which can shatter all other kinds of jewels, yet this jewel itself cannot be destroyed by anything."
In this way, Mañjuśrī,
a bodhisattva who employs skillful means disciplines all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas without falling into their states. Mañjuśrī!
Just as the fragrance of the māndārava flower pervades an entire yojana even when there is no wind,
so it is, Mañjuśrī! Though a bodhisattva who employs skillful means lacks the faculty of noble wisdom, the fragrance of their loving-kindness pervades all sentient beings.
“Mañjuśrī! Just as when one smells the fragrance of mandārava flowers, all illnesses are cured and all sufferings and afflictions cease; even so, Mañjuśrī!”
“Mañjuśrī! If all the Bodhisattvas of great kindness and great compassion should rejoice [in this], every disease of the fetters will be entirely eliminated, and there will be no further affliction.”
Just as when a Buddha appears in the world, the udumbara flower then manifests; so it is, Mañjuśrī!
When a bodhisattva appears in the world, the lotus flowers of all the Buddhas' teachings fully manifest.
“Mañjuśrī! Just as the great nāga king Anavatapta rains throughout Jambudvīpa, so it is, Mañjuśrī!”
In this way, the Bodhisattva, with the rain of the Great Dharma, universally moistens all sentient beings with an impartial mind. "Mañjuśrī!
Just as that Lake Anavatapta flows forth four rivers that fill the great ocean."
In this way, Mañjuśrī!
All bodhisattvas cause the four means of attraction to flow forth and fill the ocean of all-knowledge.
"Mañjuśrī! [he said].
Just as it is because there is a great ocean that the people of Jambudvīpa possess various precious jewels,
so too, Mañjuśrī, it is because of the bodhisattvas that all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are provided with the jewel of the Dharma of liberation.
“Mañjuśrī! All forms depend upon the four great elements.
In this same way, Mañjuśrī!”
All the dharmas possessed by a bodhisattva serve as the basis for liberation for all sentient beings.
"Mañjuśrī! It is like a great medicinal tree growing in a mountainous ravine; it cannot benefit the many people there."
In this way, Mañjuśrī!
Those who are disciplined through the teachings of the śrāvakas cannot benefit all sentient beings. “Mañjuśrī!
Just as a great medicinal tree growing within a large city benefits many people,

so it is, Mañjuśrī! Once a bodhisattva has emerged from great loving-kindness and great compassion, they do not abandon the jewel-mind of omniscience and are able to greatly benefit all sentient beings.
“Mañjuśrī! Just as the torrential force of a heavy rain does not flow for long, so it is, Mañjuśrī!”
“The power of the Śrāvakas’ teaching does not endure for long.
Mañjuśrī! It is like the springtime stream, which flows for a long duration.”
In this way, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva’s teaching of the Dharma attains long endurance in the world. "Mañjuśrī! [he said].
Just as a tree on the Snowy Mountains, though cut down, grows back again before long;
so it is, Mañjuśrī! Although the Tathāgata performs all the works of a Buddha and then enters parinirvāṇa, the seed of the Triple Gem is never severed.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!
You have now expounded upon all the immeasurable and boundless merits of the dharmas of a bodhisattva, as well as their true merits.”
World-Honored One!
This is even more rare:
that when a bodhisattva hears of these true merits, they feel neither joy nor pride.
The Buddha said,
“Subhūti! Because the root of all bodhisattvas is inherently pure, they do not rejoice or become elated upon hearing of various merits.”
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One,
how is it that the root of a bodhisattva is inherently pure?”

The Buddha said: “Subhūti! There is purity of the root of no-self; purity of the root of no-multitude; purity of the root of no-life-force; purity of the root of no-person; purity of the root of no-individual; purity of the root of no-view-of-a-body; purity of the root of no-ignorance-and-craving-for-existence; and purity of the root of no-I-and-mine.”
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One,
what is meant by ‘purity’?”
The Buddha said,
“Subhūti! That which is neither bound nor liberated is called purity.”
To be without arising and without ceasing, without going and without coming—this is called purity.

To be without false conceptualization and without discrimination; without high and without low; without action and without non-action; without darkness and without light; without affliction and without non-affliction; without bondage and without liberation; without birth-and-death and without nirvana—this is called purity.
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One,
if there is neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa, how can it be called ‘purity’?”
The Buddha said:
"Subhūti! This purity is without conceptualization regarding saṃsāra or nirvāṇa, nor is there any defiled attachment."
Subhūti! It is as if one were to say that space is purified; yet in reality, there is nothing to be removed to make space pure.
In the same way, Subhūti!
As for what is called "purity," in reality there is no dharma that can be named purity.
If, upon hearing this, one is not startled or terrified, this is called purity. Subhūti!
"Are you now pure?
Subhūti replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"I am pure because I am stainless.
The Buddha said, "Subhūti!"
"If there is no defilement, what is it that is purified? Subhūti said,
"World-Honored One!"
“I have already realized that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is pure.
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!
“Are you now able to know the nature of the dharma-realm?
Subhūti replied,
“World-Honored One!”
"If there were any dharma apart from the dharmadhātu, then the dharmadhātu could be known; yet there is no dharmadhātu that can know the dharmadhātu.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"There is not a single dharma apart from the dharmadhātu. Who, then, knows the dharmadhātu?"
At that time, Subhūti remained silent and did not answer.
Then Mañjuśrī said to Subhūti:
"Venerable One!..."
"Why do you now not answer the Tathāgata? Subhūti replied,
"Because I originally did not resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Why is this? It is because I did not originally cultivate inexhaustible and unimpeded eloquence.
Such inexhaustible and unimpeded eloquence belongs to bodhisattvas; that which is impeded and exhaustible belongs to śrāvakas.
Mañjuśrī said to Subhūti:
"In this dharmadhātu, are there obstructions or hindrances?
Subhūti replied:
"In this dharma-realm there is no obstruction and no hindrance; that which is without obstruction and without hindrance is the characteristic of the dharma-realm.
Mañjuśrī said, "Virtuous One!..."
“If the dharma-realm is unobstructed and unhindered, for what reason do you now say that there is an obstruction at the time?
Subhūti replied, “Mañjuśrī!...”
"Because I have realized and severed [all attachments], my eloquence is obstructed.
If one knows the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) yet does not realize it, then one's eloquence is unobstructed. Mañjuśrī said:
“Venerable Subhūti!
Within the dharma-realm, is there anything that can be severed?
Subhūti replied:
“Mañjuśrī! This dharma-realm cannot be severed, for all dharma-gates are entirely the dharma-realm. Mañjuśrī said:
"If all phenomena are entirely the dharma-realm, for what reason do you say, 'I have realized cessation'? Subhūti replied,
"Because the sphere of the śrāvakas is limited and finite, it is said that there is cessation at the time [of realization]."
"Because the realm of the Buddha is immeasurable, it is said to be unimpeded and unhindered. Mañjuśrī asked:
"Is there arising within the dharma-realm?"
Subhūti said: "This dharma-realm has no objective sphere; the cessation of all objective spheres is called the dharma-realm. Mañjuśrī said:
“Venerable Subhūti!
If there are no objective spheres and all objective spheres have been extinguished, for what reason do you now teach the dharma-realm within that which is without objective spheres?”
"Why do you say there are various objects? Subhūti replied,
"Did I not say before that that which is obstructed and hindered is the eloquence of the śrāvaka, while that which is unobstructed and unhindered is the eloquence of the bodhisattva?"
Mañjuśrī said: "Venerable Subhūti!
Have you not now attained unimpeded eloquence?"
"So it is, Mañjuśrī! I have attained this eloquence."
Mañjuśrī said: "Having attained unimpeded eloquence, for what reason do you remain silent?
Subhūti replied:

Because one does not know the faculties of all sentient beings, one's eloquence encounters obstructions; knowing how to enter the faculties of all sentient beings is the eloquence of a bodhisattva, and for this reason, when a bodhisattva speaks, there is no impediment.
Mañjuśrī said: "Venerable Subhūti!
When you know the dharma-realm and attain realization and eloquence, do you perceive that the sphere of knowledge has the characteristic of obstruction?"
"No, Mañjuśrī! This realm of wisdom has the characteristic of non-obstruction; it does not have the characteristic of obstruction."
Mañjuśrī said: "If the sphere of wisdom is without any characteristic of obstruction, why do you not speak and remain silent?
At that time, Subhūti spoke to the Venerable Śāriputra:
“The Buddha has always praised him as foremost in wisdom.
You may now question him; he will answer you. Śāriputra said:
"You may now speak;
I wish to hear the Dharma from you and Mañjuśrī. Subhūti said:
"I shall not speak now. Why is this?
I have seen this Mañjuśrī traveling through various Buddha-lands and preaching the Dharma before hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas, causing all the śrāvakas to fall into silence."
How could I now dare to say anything before Mañjuśrī?
Venerable Śāriputra!
To the east there is a land called Prabhāsa; therein dwells a Buddha named Prabhākara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is currently preaching the Dharma.
There was a great śrāvaka named Jñānapradīpa, foremost in wisdom.

At that time, when the Tathāgata had entered into meditative absorption, this great śrāvaka Jñānapradīpa went to the Brahma world and expounded the Dharma with a great voice, the sound of which pervaded the trichiliocosm.
I followed Mañjuśrī to that world, accompanied by immeasurable bodhisattvas and hundreds of thousands of devaputras who attended upon Mañjuśrī for the sake of hearing the Dharma.
At that time, Mañjuśrī dwelt in the Ābhāsvara Heaven and emitted a great sound that was heard throughout the trichiliocosm.

At that time, the great śrāvaka Jñānapradīpa, unable to endure hearing such a great voice, fell from his high position; his heart was struck with terror and the hair on his body stood on end, so he immediately went to where the Buddha Prabhūtaratna was.
Having arrived, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, asked about this matter:
“World-Honored One!
Who has produced such a terrifying sound?”
"When I heard this sound, I could not endure it; I fell from above like a small bird blown by a whirlwind.
At that time, the Buddha said to the bhikṣu Jñānapradīpa:

"There is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī who has manifested great supernormal powers and come to this land, desiring to see me and to make offerings, pay respect, honor, and praise me."
Abiding in the Ābhāsvara Heaven, they emit a great sound; this sound pervades the Buddha-worlds of the trichiliocosm, completely obscuring all the palaces of Māra.
Then the śrāvaka Jñānapradīpa addressed the Buddha Prabhāketu, saying:
"I wish to see this great mahāsattva Mañjuśrī.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata Prabhāketu manifested a sign for Mañjuśrī, causing Mañjuśrī, together with the assembly of bodhisattvas and his retinue of devas, to come to the presence of the Buddha.
Having arrived, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having manifested a lion throne made of lotuses,
sat down to one side. Then, the great śrāvaka Jñānapradīpa asked Mañjuśrī,
"For what benefit have you come to this land?"
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī said to the great virtuous one, Jyotirdhvaja:
"I have come here now in order to see the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, to pay him homage, to attend upon him, to inquire after his well-being, and to request the Dharma."
Jñānapradīpa asked:
“Mañjuśrī, what is meant by ‘pure vision of the Buddha’?”
How does one pay homage to the Buddha?
How does one draw near to him?
How does one inquire after his well-being?
"How do you inquire? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Great Virtuous One, Jyotirdhvaja!"
If one sees the purity of the Dharma, this is called seeing the purity of the Buddha.

Whether in body or mind, neither bowing down nor looking up, but abiding upright without bending or tilting, unmoving and unshakable with a tranquil mind, practicing the practice of tranquility—O Mahāpuṇya-dīpa!

This is called paying homage to the Buddha. If one does not observe oneself nor observe others; does not observe the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Sangha; does not observe difficulty or ease; does not observe action or non-action; being of one essence and one body, with all Buddha-bodies equally entering the Dharma-body, seeing one's own body as likewise entering the nature of phenomena (dharmatā); seeing as if not seeing, with neither near nor far—O Virtuous One, Lamp of Wisdom!
This is what is called drawing near to the Buddha.

If one practices and inquires regarding that which the Tathāgata has performed, rather than not practicing, and does not perceive any dharma that is not being practiced; if one perceives both oneself and all dharmas as entering into practice; if the mind of inquiry is settled and free from distraction; if the inquirer, the object of inquiry, and the dharma of inquiry are all unobtainable and free from attachment; and if they cannot be found when sought within the three periods of time—such is the pure inquiry of these three spheres, O Great Virtuous One, Lamp of Wisdom!
This is what is called inquiring after the Buddha’s well-being.

When engaging in dialogue while coming and going, one does not seek out faults; one accords with the questions asked and receives the Tathāgata’s seal of approval. The great assembly rejoices and does not envy the inquiries of others.

When there is something to be asked, it causes immeasurable sentient beings to give rise to the adornment of the Path, even unto the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), O Great Virtuous One, Lamp of Wisdom!
"This is what is called questioning the Buddha.
Then, the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna praised Mañjuśrī:
"Excellent, excellent!"

Mañjuśrī! One should view the Tathāgata in this way; one should pay homage to him in this way; one should attend upon him in this way; one should inquire after his well-being in this way; and one should pose questions to him in this way.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī asked the bhikṣu Jñānapradīpa:
"Virtuous Jñānapradīpa!
How do you perceive the Buddha?"
How does one pay homage to the Buddha?
How does one draw near to him?
How does one inquire after his well-being?
"How do you inquire?
Wisdom-Lamp replied, "Mañjuśrī!..."
"What you have asked is not within my domain.
I have spoken thus only because I heard it from others according to their voices. Mañjuśrī said:
“O Great Virtuous One, Jñānapradīpa!
If you do not understand this, how can you attain liberation of mind?
Jñānapradīpa replied:
"Because of the Noble Truths, the mind attains liberation.
Mañjuśrī asked, "What is meant by 'Noble Truth'?"
Jñānapradīpa replied:
"To practice alone without a companion is called the Noble Truth.
He asked again:
"If practicing alone without a companion is called the Noble Truth, how can one attain noble liberation through the mind that perceives equality?
He replied: "Mañjuśrī!..."
"I speak based on conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), not from the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārtha).
He asked again:
"Does this conventional truth enter into ultimate truth?"
He replied: "Mañjuśrī!
If one does not enter therein, it is not the ultimate truth."
He asked again:
"O Jñānapradīpa!
Why do you say that this is spoken according to conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and not according to ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya)?"
"If the conventional truth enters into the ultimate truth, they are then a single truth, namely, the ultimate truth.
At that time, Jñānapradīpa said: "Mañjuśrī!..."
"Bodhisattvas who have newly begun their practice will feel alarm and fear upon hearing what you have said.
Mañjuśrī replied, "Virtuous Devaratna!..."
"If even you are struck with fear and dread, how much more so for those who are beginners!
Jñānapradīpa replied,
"There is absolutely no one capable of striking me with fear."
Mañjuśrī said: "Virtuous One!
Is it not the case that one who is terrified of birth and death attains liberation of mind?"
Jñānapradīpa said:
“Mañjuśrī! Through fear and wearying aversion, the mind attains liberation.”
Mañjuśrī said: "Therefore,
O Great Virtuous Jyotirdhvaja, I say that even those who have long practiced are terrified, let alone those who are beginners."
Jñānapradīpa asked:
"Mañjuśrī, how does a bodhisattva attain liberation?"
Mañjuśrī replied,
"Fearlessness and non-repulsion are the liberation of a bodhisattva. He asked:
“Mañjuśrī! Regarding your statement that one attains liberation through neither fear nor aversion, what is the meaning of this?
Mañjuśrī replied:

"A Bodhisattva does not fear the hosts of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Māras; a Bodhisattva does not weary of [working for] all sentient beings in saṃsāra; a Bodhisattva does not fear the accumulation of roots of goodness; a Bodhisattva does not weary of the accumulation of the adornment of wisdom. For this reason, I have said: through non-fear and non-weariness, the mind attains liberation."
At that time, there were various devaputras in the assembly who scattered various flowers as an offering to the youth Mañjuśrī and spoke thus in praise:
"If one sees Mañjuśrī wherever he dwells, it is as if seeing the Buddha;
in whatever place he preaches the Dharma, one should conceive the thought that it is a stūpa."
"If there are sentient beings who hear this Dharma, you should know that such persons have already gathered all virtues.
Then Mañjuśrī said to the bhikṣu Jñānapradīpa,
"The Buddha has declared that you, Great Virtue, are foremost in wisdom."
Is this wisdom conditioned or unconditioned?
If it were conditioned,
it would possess the three characteristics of arising, ceasing, and abiding.
"If it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), then it lacks the three characteristics. Zhideng replied:
"Because they cultivate the unconditioned, the Buddha calls them 'noble ones' (*ārya*)."
Mañjuśrī asked: "Virtuous Devaratna!
Can this unconditioned state be cultivated?"
"No, Mañjuśrī. Mañjuśrī spoke again:
“How is it, Venerable One, that you say the cultivation of the unconditioned is called ‘noble’?
At that time, the great śrāvaka Jñānapradīpa remained silent.
Then, the Tathāgata Prabhāsa said to Mañjuśrī:
"Please preach the Dharma-door so that all those in this assembly shall not regress from the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"All dharmas are gates of tranquility; all verbal expressions are gates of tranquility, because they demonstrate tranquility.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Dharmavīra who sat in the assembly and asked Mañjuśrī:
"Is that which the Tathāgata has spoken regarding greed, hatred, and delusion a gate of tranquility that demonstrates tranquility?
Mañjuśrī replied,
"Noble son!..."
"From what do these greed, hatred, and delusion arise?
He replied, "Mañjuśrī!"
"It arises from deluded thought.
Mañjuśrī asked again,
"Where does this deluded thought abide?"
He replied: "Mañjuśrī,
they abide in perversion."
Mañjuśrī asked:
"Where does this inversion abide?
He replied:
"Mañjuśrī! You dwell in improper reflection.
Mañjuśrī asked again:
"Where does improper reflection abide?
He replied, "Mañjuśrī!..."
"They dwell in 'I' and 'mine.
Mañjuśrī asked again,
"In what place do 'I' and 'mine' dwell?"
He replied:
"Mañjuśrī, they abide in the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi)."
Mañjuśrī asked again:
"Where does this view of a self abide?
He replied:
"Mañjuśrī! You abide in the view of a self.
Mañjuśrī asked again:
"Where does this one who possesses the view of self abide?
He replied, "Mañjuśrī!..."
For one who holds the view of a self, there is no place of abiding;
there is no locus that serves as the basis for the view of a self. Why is this?
"Yet this 'self' cannot be found at all, even when sought throughout the ten directions, much less in any specific location.
Mañjuśrī asked again: "Good son!"
"If a dharma cannot be found when sought throughout the ten directions,
what gate is this? He replied,
"Mañjuśrī!..."
"It has no gate whatsoever.
Mañjuśrī asked again:
"Good son!..."
"But is there any gateway to this tranquility?
He replied, "Mañjuśrī!
This, too, is without a gate. Good son!
For this reason, I say that all dharmas are the gate of tranquility.
"All verbal expressions are gates to tranquility; they reveal tranquility.
When this Dharma was spoken, eight hundred bodhisattvas attained the stage of patience (*kṣānti*).
Having extensively expounded the Dharma, Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One Prabhūtaratna, and departed from the assembly.
"Therefore, Śāriputra,
you should know that there is no śrāvaka or bodhisattva capable of exhausting Mañjuśrī’s eloquence.
How would I dare to engage in any discussion with Mañjuśrī?"
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
"Venerable sir,
what further miraculous transformations of Mañjuśrī have you seen as he travels through the various Buddha-fields?"
Śāriputra said: "Venerable Subhūti!
In the past, I once traveled with Mañjuśrī through various Buddha-lands in the western direction."
He saw a buddha-field where a great conflagration had broken out; within those flames, Mañjuśrī created a lattice of lotuses and passed through it.

Again, he saw a buddha-field filled with the calamity of fire, yet Mañjuśrī passed through its midst. When this fire touched people, it was like applying solid sandalwood paste to the body or lying upon Kāśi cloth—so soft, harmonious, and exceedingly pleasant.

Furthermore, there are buddha-fields that are empty and devoid of anything; Mañjuśrī transforms them into Brahmā palaces and, entering into meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), passes through them.

Again, there are buddha-fields that are extremely narrow, where sentient beings commit various evil deeds; as Mañjuśrī passes through them, he causes them all to cease their actions and refrain from evil, bringing about the awakening-wisdom of compassion (*bodhicitta-karuṇā*). [He thinks: "I shall attain the Unsurpassed Right Path and preach the Dharma for the sake of severing the greed, hatred, and delusion of sentient beings, so that all beings may attain the Samādhi of Compassion. This is called the bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the awakening-wisdom of compassion.
"Venerable Subhūti!
At that time, I witnessed these events.
Furthermore, while dwelling in solitude, I had this thought: "
“Whatever supernatural powers Mañjuśrī possesses are equal to my own supernatural powers; there is no difference between them.
Having known my thoughts, Mañjuśrī immediately took me to travel through various Buddha-lands until we reached a land ravaged by the calamity of fire, where he said to me:
“Pass through this place by means of your own supernormal power.”
At that time, having extinguished this fire entirely through the power of my supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*), Mañjuśrī and I passed beyond this world-system after seven days and nights.
Having passed it, we arrived at a second trichiliocosm—a world-system of the calamity of fire—which was twice as vast. Having stayed there, Mañjuśrī spoke to me, saying:
"By whose supernatural power did you pass beyond this world-system?"
I then replied: "Mañjuśrī! By means of your supernatural power, pass beyond these worlds."

At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī focused his mind upon what lay ahead;
by the supernatural power of a bodhisattva, in a single thought-moment he created a network of lotuses that completely covered the fire, and having passed through it, he spoke to me, saying:
"Venerable Śāriputra!..."
"What do you think?
Is your supernatural power superior, or is mine?"
I then replied:
"Mañjuśrī! Is the king of the garuḍas swift in his flight?"
"Is it because of the small birds' haste?
Mañjuśrī then asked me in return:
"What do you think?"
"Of these two birds, which one is faster? I then replied:
"My spiritual power is like that of the small bird; your spiritual power is superior, swifter, and extraordinary, surpassing even the golden-winged garuḍa."
Mañjuśrī then said to me:
"Venerable Śāriputra!
You were dwelling alone in thought:..."
“Mañjuśrī’s spiritual power and my own spiritual power are equal and without distinction.
I replied again: “They cannot be compared.”
Mañjuśrī asked, "How do you know this?
I immediately replied:
"Śrāvakas do not sever their habitual tendencies; therefore, I have originally regarded that which is unequal as equal.
Mañjuśrī said: "Excellent, excellent!"
"It is as you have said,
Śāriputra! Long ago,
in a past age, there were two rishis dwelling by the shore of the great ocean."
One was named Kāma-dharmā and the other was named Brahmā-datta.
At that time, Kāma-dharmā attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), while the seer Brahmā-datta was able to travel through the air by the power of his incantations.
Then those two men, each by their own power, crossed the great ocean and returned to their dwelling places.
At that time, the seer Brahmadatta spoke these words:
"The supernatural power of the Dharma and my own supernatural power are equal and no different."
Again, at another time, he traveled from this shore of the ocean to the other shore, arriving at the island of the rākṣasas. At that time, the rākṣasas there produced the sounds of flutes and pipes.
When the seer Brahmadatta heard these sounds, he fell from the sky, losing his power of incantations.
At that time, the ṛṣi Kāma, out of compassion for Brahmāyus, took him by his right arm and led him to his dwelling place.
"Venerable Śāriputra,
what do you think?"
Is this Brahmāyus, the seer, anyone other than you?
Do not view him as another; he is indeed your own self.
And I am that very seer, Kāma-dhenu.
Śāriputra! At that time you also took the unequal as equal, and now you again take the unequal as equal. Why is this?
"It is because of their biased views.
At that time, Śāriputra spoke again to Subhūti:

"I further recall that after Mañjuśrī and I had traveled through hundreds of thousands of Buddha-fields in the southern direction, there was a land named Sarvavyūha, where the Buddha was named Ratnamahādeva; Mañjuśrī and I both went to that land together."
Once Mañjuśrī had arrived there, he spoke to me, saying:
"Do you now see this buddha-field?
Do you see all the lands through which we have passed?"
I replied, "I have seen them.
He then questioned me further:
"What do you see in all these lands? I then replied:
"In some I see them filled with water; in others, filled with fire; in others, the void; and in others, abundance and joy."
Mañjuśrī spoke again:
"How do you see it?
At that time, I replied:

"If one sees water full [to the brim], one says one sees water; if one sees fire full, one says one sees fire; if one sees the realm of space, one says one sees the realm of space; if one sees abundance and prosperity, one says one sees abundance and prosperity."
Mañjuśrī said, "The realm you perceive is such as this.
At that time, I asked:
“Mañjuśrī! How do you, in turn, perceive the various buddha-fields?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"The world of empty space is the world of all Buddhas.
Why is this? Because you are deluded by illusion, you perceive it as filled with water, filled with fire, the realm of emptiness, and abundant prosperity."
Śāriputra! All that you perceive is individually unreal and characterized by arising and ceasing.
The world of empty space does not exist through causes and conditions; its nature is one of stable abiding.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
Though adventitious afflictions defile the mind, the nature of the mind can never be defiled.
O Venerable Śāriputra!
Just as the fires of the kalpa-ending conflagration, blazing for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges,
can never burn empty space; so too, Śāriputra,

even if each and every sentient being were to commit the unwholesome karma of the heinous crimes for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, their fundamental nature of mind could never be defiled.

Śāriputra! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family can understand that the nature of this dharma-realm is pure, being free from the shrouds and entanglements and devoid of the defilements and fetters that can afflict the mind, this is called the Dharma-gate of the absence of shrouds and entanglements.

If one relies on this gate, all phenomena are incapable of covering; one understands that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is pure, and ultimately there is no phenomenon whatsoever capable of obscuring the mind.
"Venerable Subhūti! Such were the supernatural transformations and the preaching of the Dharma by Mañjuśrī.
When I witnessed those various miraculous feats, even the bodhisattvas could not fathom them, let alone the śrāvakas."
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda spoke again to Śāriputra:

"The power of birth and death is the power of Māra; the power of the patience of non-arising—which is without birth, without cessation, and without all conditioned formations—is the power of a bodhisattva.

When King Māra Pāpīyān preached this Dharma, five hundred devaputras among the celestial host conceived the aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and twelve hundred bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Pāpīyān! That which is called "poison" refers to greed, hatred, and delusion;
as for those who are well-praised and disciplined within the Dharma, it is impossible for them to give poison to others.
Furthermore, Māra Pāpīyān!
That which is called "poison" refers to ignorance and craving for existence; the view of a self and what belongs to a self; the view of causelessness; the view of name-and-form;
the view of attachment, aversion, and hatred; the view of a self and the view of sentient beings; and the views of all hindrances and entanglements.
They become conceptually attached to the aggregates (*skandha*), giving rise to pride regarding their spiritual lineage (*gotra-māna*);
they cling to the sense bases (*āyatana*), constantly dwelling within the three realms, being bound to and attached to their physical support, guarding it, and engaging in grasping and rejecting;

whether coming or going, they are fondly attached to the body, stubbornly clinging to life, harboring impure thoughts, delighting in a defiled mind, frequently giving rise to various transgressions, and acting in opposition to the nature of causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
They sever the views of annihilationism and eternalism; they harbor flattery, crookedness, arrogance, and false conceptualization;
they manifest deceit and hypocrisy; they cling to their nests and dens; they appear and disappear, expanding and contracting, trembling in fear of emptiness;

they conceive thoughts of falling within the state of non-conception; they conceive thoughts of birth and death within the state of non-action; and they give rise to fear within the state of non-attachment.

They conceive the notion of being born within saṃsāra; they conceive the notion of bondage regarding the arising of birth and death; they do not conceive the notion of crossing over within the flow of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*);
they conceive the notion that things are contrary to the Dharma regarding the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*); they conceive the notion of right view within wrong views;

they conceive the notion of a virtuous friend regarding evil associates (*pāpamitra*); they oppose the Buddha, slander the Dharma, and treat the Saṅgha with contempt; and they do not abandon arrogance.
Pride increases contention; one perceives the real as unreal and the unreal as real; one conceives of sensual pleasures as meritorious;
one gives rise to delusion within conditioned phenomena; one fails to see the faults in the activities of birth and death;
and one conceives of fear toward nirvāṇa.
Pāpīyan! Such dharmas as these are called "poisons" within the Sublime Dharma.
Within the Buddha’s True Dharma, no such things exist.

World-Honored One!
If there are sentient beings who hear this sutra, they shall never again commit indolence or unrighteous acts, nor shall they ever again perform the various evil deeds of Māra.
