A great, brilliant physician gave that man some clarified butter to drink, and his feverish illness was immediately cured and ceased;
he no longer spoke falsely. What do you think?
"Are there any devas or ghosts departing from here? I replied, "No."
"Mañjuśrī! Because of drinking the clarified butter, the feverish illness was cured. "Venerable Kāśyapa!"
"Does this skilled physician bring great benefit to them?
I replied, "It is so."
"Mañjuśrī! Mañjuśrī replied, "Venerable Kāśyapa!"
The world is thus: afflicted by the fever of inversion, it perceives a self where there is no self.
Dwelling in the perception of a self, it wanders through birth and death.

Therefore, the Tathāgata appears in the world and, according to their physical forms and the Dharma-gates they should understand, he brings about the realization that the perception of a self is an inversion; for the sake of those sentient beings, he expounds the Dharma.
Having heard the Dharma, one eliminates all conceptualizations and remains free from attachment.
Having understood and resolved these conceptualizations, one transcends all currents and reaches the other shore; this is called nirvāṇa.
"Venerable Kāśyapa,
what do you think? Within this,
is there any self, sentient being, life-span, nourished person, or individual who can attain parinirvāṇa?"
I then replied: "No, Mañjuśrī!"
Mañjuśrī said: "Venerable Kāśyapa!

It is for this benefit that the Tathāgata appears in the world; it is solely to demonstrate the perception of equality, not for the sake of arising, nor for the sake of ceasing, but solely to bring about the understanding that afflictions are unreal."
I then said: "Mañjuśrī! What the bodhisattvas do is truly rare and difficult:

namely, to contemplate and know that the nature of sentient beings is ultimately quiescent, yet for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, they do not abandon their adornments, nor do they sink into or emerge from [nirvāṇa]."
"The nature of sentient beings is ultimately nirvana, yet they are still able to give rise to great vows as adornment.
Mañjuśrī said, "Virtuous Kāśyapa!..."
"The adornments of a bodhisattva are identical to suchness.
I then asked Mañjuśrī:
"I pray that you will explain the great adornment undertaken by a bodhisattva."
Mañjuśrī said: “Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have set out in the great armor have thirty-two [aspects].
What are these thirty-two?”
The bodhisattva undertakes the great adornment by embracing immeasurable births and deaths, because they are like dreams and empty in nature.
The bodhisattva undertakes the great adornment by bringing immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa, because there is no mark of a self.
The Bodhisattva makes the great adornment of serving and making offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, because they share the same characteristics as the Dharma-body.
The Bodhisattva makes the great adornment of hearing and receiving all Buddha-dharmas, because they have the characteristics of an echo.
A bodhisattva donates the great armor of protecting all Buddha-dharmas because they understand and penetrate the mark of equality of all phenomena.
A bodhisattva donates the great armor of subduing all māras because the nature and characteristics of all fetters (*saṃyojana*) are pure.
The Bodhisattva dons the great armor of subduing all non-Buddhists, because he causes those who hold views of existence and non-existence to understand the characteristics of dependent origination.
The Bodhisattva dons the great armor of relinquishing everything, because he relinquishes all things without remainder.
The Bodhisattva donning the great armor by gathering the merit of the precepts and dhūtas, because they are devoid of the mark of activity.
The Bodhisattva donning the great armor through the power of patience, because they are devoid of the mark of injury.
The bodhisattva’s diligence constitutes a great adornment, because he understands and realizes the mark of tranquility within body and mind.
The bodhisattva’s all-encompassing meditative concentrations and liberations constitute a great adornment, because he has relinquished all marks of dependence.
The Bodhisattva donates the great armor of unimpeded *prajñāpāramitā*, because it purifies and eliminates the marks of ignorance, delusion, and views.
The Bodhisattva donates the great armor of skillful means (*upāya*), because it manifests all the marks of what is to be done.
The Bodhisattva’s great kindness gives rise to great adornment, because it has the characteristic of space.
The Bodhisattva’s great compassion gives rise to great adornment, because they understand and know that the five realms of existence have the characteristic of emptiness.
The Bodhisattva’s great joy gives rise to great adornment, because it is free from the signs of sorrow and affliction.
The Bodhisattva’s great equanimity gives rise to great adornment, because it is detached from the signs of suffering and pleasure.
The Bodhisattva cultivates and fulfills the wisdom of great supernormal powers and gives rise to the great armor, because he perceives liberation within his own palm as being free from doubt.
The Bodhisattva does not dwell on the selflessness of all phenomena and gives rise to the great armor, because he does not fear falling into the states of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
The Bodhisattva contemplates the aggregates as being like hostile bandits and thus dons the great armor, because he knows them to be illusory in nature.
The Bodhisattva contemplates the four great elements as being like venomous snakes and thus dons the great armor, because they share the same characteristic as the Dharma-realm.
The Bodhisattva contemplates the sense-bases as being like an empty village and thus generates the great armor, because he recognizes the characteristics of hostile bandits.
The Bodhisattva does not cling to the three realms and thus generates the great armor, because they have no nesting place or lair.
The Bodhisattva resolutely undertakes the great adornment of grasping all states of existence because they possess the characteristic of both being and non-being.
The Bodhisattva, through great compassion, undertakes the great adornment because it possesses the characteristic of non-retrogression.
The Bodhisattva dons the great armor as a Great Physician-King, because he bestows the medicine of the Dharma according to whatever ailments sentient beings may have.
The Bodhisattva dons the great armor as a Great Caravan Leader, because he shows and guides them toward the path that leads out [of saṃsāra] via the three vehicles.
The Bodhisattva initiates the great adornment by not severing the lineage of the Three Jewels, because he understands the characteristic of repaying the kindness of all Buddhas.

The Bodhisattva initiates the great adornment by knowing that the nature of all phenomena is non-arising, because he attains the characteristic of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

The Bodhisattva dons the great armor in order to attain the stage of non-retrogression, because he abandons all fetters within the triple world and relinquishes the characteristics of the stages of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha.

The Bodhisattva adorns the site of enlightenment by giving rise to the great adornment, because through wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment, they understand the characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are.
Thus it is, Kāśyapa!
These are called the thirty-two kinds of great adornments undertaken by Bodhisattvas.

If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva adorns himself with these adornments, even the fundamental nature of the four great elements could be changed, yet this Bodhisattva will never regress from the unsurpassed path.
I then replied: "If one does not yet retreat even when setting out in great adornment, how much less so for thirty-two? Mañjuśrī!"
"In the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, there is no adornment.
Mañjuśrī said, "Venerable Kāśyapa!..."
Therefore, śrāvakas lack the great adornment, even down to the very name,
which the bodhisattvas possess.
Venerable Kāśyapa, what do you think?
Suppose there were a great warrior, well-adorned with various armor and weapons and wielding a sharp sword, and another person who was timid and only roughly adorned.
Could these two forms of adornment be compared to one another?
I replied, "No. Mañjuśrī said:
"For this reason, Venerable Kāśyapa, the adornments of a bodhisattva are not possessed by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
When these words concerning the great adornment of the bodhisattva were spoken, twelve thousand devaputras conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.
"Therefore, Śāriputra,
I see that the inconceivable supernormal powers and wisdom of the youth Mañjuśrī are thus immeasurable.
At that time, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said to Śāriputra:
"I have also witnessed what the youth Mañjuśrī has done.
Once, in the past, the Buddha was staying at the Āmra Grove in Vaiśālī together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus."
At that time, Satyaka Nirgrantha-putra was residing within the great city of Vaiśālī together with a retinue of sixty thousand, receiving offerings and respect.
I entered into samādhi and observed this Nirgrantha; at that moment, I saw that there were hundreds of thousands of Nirgranthas who were ready to be transformed.
I then went there and preached the Dharma for them;
yet they did not listen attentively with a virtuous heart, but instead treated me with contempt and laughter, uttering coarse and evil words.
My efforts were thus in vain during those three months, as not a single person was transformed. When the three months had passed, my heart was displeased, and I abandoned them and departed.

At that time, Mañjuśrī immediately manifested as five hundred followers of other paths, acting as their own teachers, and leading five hundred disciples to the place where Satyaka Nirgranthaputra was. He prostrated at his feet and addressed Satyaka, saying:
"I have long heard of the fame and virtue of the Great Master; therefore, I have come from afar to Vaiśālī."
"You are my teacher and I am your disciple.
I pray that you will accept me and grant me your compassionate instruction, so that I may not see the śramaṇa Gautama and may not hear his contrary teachings."
Saccaka replied:
"Excellent, excellent!
Your intention is pure; before long, you shall understand my method of discipline."
At that time, Satyaka immediately issued a proclamation to his own followers:
"These five hundred māṇavas shall from this day forward dwell together in harmony and consult one another; whatever they may say, you must receive it with single-minded attention."

At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī and his five hundred transformed disciples sat down in order to listen; they received and practiced the Nigaṇṭha precepts, yet their dignified deportment was far superior to theirs.
From time to time, they praised the merits of the Triple Gem and also extolled the merits of Satyaka, causing the hearts of those people to become closely attached to one another.
On another occasion, knowing that the assembly had gathered, Mañjuśrī spoke these words:
"In the incantations, scriptures, and *Videha-sūtras* that we practice, when we read or recite them, the various merits of the śramaṇa Gautama appear within our own texts."
This śramaṇa Gautama possesses the merit of true dharmas. Why is this?

This śramaṇa Gautama was born into a perfected lineage; his parents are pure and he belongs to the clan of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), his body adorned with the marks of a hundred blessings.
Furthermore, it is heard that at the time of his birth, the great earth shook, and Śakra and Brahmā attended him as he took seven steps by himself and spoke these words:
"I am the most excellent in all the worlds; I am the greatest in the world. Now I shall bring an end to all birth and death."

In the sky, two waters spontaneously appeared for Śakra and Brahmā to bathe him; the musical instruments of humans and devas resounded without being struck; a great radiance was emitted, illuminating the entire world, and extinguishing the suffering of all evil realms by restoring sight and hearing to the deaf and blind.
At that time, all sentient beings were free from the afflictions of the fetters and dwelt in peace and unconditioned bliss.
The marks of a brahmin [prophesied]:
"If he does not leave the household life, he will become a wheel-turning monarch; if he does leave the household life, he will become a Dharma King."

That Gautama, having renounced the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch to leave the household life and cultivate the Way, subdued ten billion māras at the site of enlightenment, realized the path of Bodhi, and turned the wondrous Wheel of Dharma.
Neither śramaṇas nor brahmins, nor Māra, nor Brahmā, nor anyone in the world—whether gods or humans—can overturn it.
What is spoken is true and authentic, excellent in the beginning, middle, and end.
What is excellence in the beginning?
It refers to wholesome conduct of body, and wholesome conduct of speech and mind.
What is excellence in the middle?
One trains in superior ethical discipline, superior concentration, and superior wisdom.
What is "good in the end"?
It refers to the dharma-gate of liberation through the emptiness samādhi, the dharma-gate of liberation through the signless samādhi, and the dharma-gate of liberation through the wishless samādhi.

Furthermore, "good in the beginning" refers to faith, aspiration, and heedfulness; "good in the middle" refers to concentration and mindfulness on a single object; and "good in the end" refers to excellent and sublime wisdom. Furthermore, "good in the beginning" refers to unshakable faith in the Buddha;
"good in the middle" refers to unshakable faith in the Dharma; and "good in the end" refers to unshakable faith in the Noble Sangha who have attained the fruits [of the path].

Furthermore, "good in the beginning" refers to hearing the Dharma from others; "good in the middle" refers to practicing with right mindfulness; and "good in the end" refers to attaining noble right view.

Furthermore, "good in the beginning" refers to knowing suffering and abandoning its origin; "good in the middle" refers to practicing the Noble Eightfold Path; and "good in the end" refers to realizing cessation.
This is called the Śrāvaka’s excellence in the beginning, middle, and end.
“What is the Bodhisattva’s excellence in the beginning, middle, and end?

Not abandoning the mind of enlightenment is called excellence in the beginning; not thinking of the Lesser Vehicle is called excellence in the middle; dedicating [merit] toward all-knowledge is called excellence in the end.”

Furthermore, "good in the beginning" means having a mind of equanimity and loving-kindness toward all sentient beings; "good in the middle" means giving rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings and employing whatever skillful means; and "good in the end" means being equal in joy and relinquishment.

Furthermore, "good in the beginning" means subduing stinginess and greed, abandoning the breaking of precepts, distancing oneself from anger, severing laziness, not dwelling in a distracted mind, and destroying ignorance. "Good in the middle" refers to generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. "Good in the end" means dedicating all the *pāramitās* toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

Furthermore, "good in the beginning" refers to teaching and transforming sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); "good in the middle" refers to protecting the true Dharma without begrudging one's own body or life; and "good in the end" refers to employing skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) so as not to fall into fixed realization (*samyaktvaniyāma*).

Furthermore, "good in the beginning" refers to maintaining a mind that, like the earth, upholds all bodhisattva practices without abandoning them; "good in the middle" refers to knowing when to advance and when to retreat through skillful means, thereby abiding in the stage of non-retrogression; and "good in the end" refers to the consecration into the position of true sovereignty within a single lifetime.
"This is called the Bodhisattva’s goodness in the beginning, middle, and end.
*The Mahāvaipulya Ratnakaranda Sūtra*, Middle Fascicle;
*The Mahāvaipulya Ratnakaranda Sūtra*, Lower Fascicle.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty:
"At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī gradually revealed such True Dharma among the assembly of non-Buddhists,

causing five hundred non-Buddhists to be far removed from dust and defilement and attain the purity of the Dharma-eye, and causing eight thousand non-Buddhists to resolve their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path."
At that time, the five hundred followers manifested by the youth Mañjuśrī prostrated themselves before Mañjuśrī with their five limbs touching the ground and spoke these words:
"Homage to the Buddha!"
"Homage to the Buddha!

When the other non-Buddhist practitioners who had not yet attained faith or understanding saw the five hundred young brahmins speaking these words, they also all imitated them by prostrating themselves with their five limbs touching the ground and saying:
"Homage to the Buddha!"
“Namo Buddhāya!
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra gave a mandārava flower to each of the people and spoke these words:
“You may use this to make an offering to the Buddha.”
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī, together with the great assembly, respectfully surrounded him as they approached the place where the World-Honored One was.
Having arrived, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the great assembly also paid homage to the Buddha and withdrew to stand to one side.
Then, the disciples of the Nirgrantha heretics, having scattered mandārava flowers as an offering to the Buddha, circumambulated him three times to the right and stood to one side.
The young brahmin, who had been transformed by Mañjuśrī, sustained by the power of Mañjuśrī, said:
"World-Honored One!
We have not come now for the sake of seeing the Buddha."
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is called the Dharma-body.
World-Honored One!
We do not come for the sake of listening to the Dharma. Why is this?
That which cannot be heard is called the Dharma.
World-Honored One!
We do not act for the sake of the Sangha’s virtue. Why is this?
"Because the Tathāgata and the noble Saṃgha cultivate the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
World-Honored One!
We do not act for the sake of merit."
Why is this? Because within this dharma-realm there are no merits to be praised; it is thus that all things are extolled.
World-Honored One!
We do not practice for the sake of cultivating the path. Why is this?
Because all dharmas are themselves the ultimate path.
World-Honored One!
We do not seek to attain the fruits [of the path]. Why is this?
"World-Honored One, that which is without leaves, flowers, or fruit is called liberation.
We do not seek to know suffering."
Why is this? Because liberation is defined as being free from these two modes of conduct,
World-Honored One!
We do not act for the sake of severing the origin [of suffering]. Why is this?
Because all phenomena are ultimately without conjunction.
"Bhagavān!
We do not seek to realize cessation. Why is this? "
"World-Honored One, because all dharmas are ultimately extinguished,
we do not cultivate the path."
Why is this? Because it is free from existence and non-existence,
World-Honored One!
We do not cultivate the foundations of mindfulness.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are free from the categories of the possible and the impossible.
World-Honored One!
We do not practice right abandonment. Why is this?
“Because all dharmas are free from the activities of the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate,
O Bhagavān,
we do not employ the supernormal powers.”
Why is this? Because all dharmas have neither coming nor going,
World-Honored One!
We do not act for the sake of the sense faculties. Why is this?
Because all sense faculties have the nature of detachment.
World-Honored One!
We do not act out of power. Why is this?
"Because all dharmas are neither powerful nor powerless,
World-Honored One,
we do not strive for awakening."
Why is this? Because in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no cognition (*buddhi*).
World-Honored One!
We do not practice for the sake of the true path. Why is this?
Because there is no going to the end of the world.
World-Honored One!
We do not practice for the sake of meditative concentration. Why is this?
Because there is no agitation within the state of constant tranquil concentration,
World-Honored One,
we do not cultivate wisdom derived from reflection.
For what reason?
Because supramundane wisdom is free from all admixture.
World-Honored One!
We do not possess the three types of supernormal knowledge. Why is this?
Because such objects of knowledge ultimately do not exist for either of us.
"World-Honored One!
We do not seek liberation. Why is this?"
"World-Honored One! Because our natures and dharmas are bound by evil,
we are not śramaṇas."
Why is this? Because one who is free from the accumulation of fetters is called a śramaṇa,
World-Honored One!
We do not consider ourselves to be brahmins. Why is this?
One who has severed all forms and names is called a brahmin.
World-Honored One!
We do not consider ourselves bhikṣus. Why is this?
Because the nature of phenomena is indestructible,
O Bhagavān,
we do not constitute the "other shore."
Why is this? Because the six sense bases are eternally extinguished,
World-Honored One!
We do not practice fewness of desires.
Why is this? Because we do not possess even the slightest bit of desire.
World-Honored One!
We do not practice contentment. Why is this?
"Because dharmas are without grasping,
World-Honored One,
we do not seek tranquility."
Why is this? Because there is no loss of body or mind,
World-Honored One!
We do not act as kinsmen. Why is this?
Because we do not dwell together with those within the three realms.
World-Honored One!
We do not associate with close friends. Why is this?
"Because we do not perceive duality,
World-Honored One,
we are not forest-dwellers."
For what reason? Because,
World-Honored One, all conditioned phenomena within the three realms are themselves forest-dwellers (āraṇyaka).
We do not cultivate non-contention. Why is this?
To be solitary and without companion is what is called non-contention.
World-Honored One!
We do not go for alms. Why is this?
"World-Honored One, because we have forever severed the characteristics of food,
we do not fear any of the conditioned phenomena of birth and death."
Why is this? Because they do not perceive reality,
World-Honored One!
We do not fear or avoid greed, hatred, and delusion.
Why is this? Because we are free from false imaginings and all conceptual discriminations.
World-Honored One,
we do not diligently strive to sever the fetters. Why is this?
All afflictions are by nature suchness (tathatā), for they are without defilement.
World-Honored One!
We do not emerge from the view of self (ātma-dṛṣṭi).
Why is this? Because one's own body is not the [true] body,
World-Honored One!
Our various impure views are not [impure].
Why is this? Because the nature of all afflictions is the mark of suchness (tathatā).
World-Honored One!
We do not sever our inverted views. Why is this?
Because our nature is eternally blissful, self, pure, and liberated.
World-Honored One!
We do not cross over the various torrents.
Why is this? Because one does not perceive this shore or the other shore,
World-Honored One.
We do not sever the five hindrances. Why is this?
Because these hindrances are already pierced through by liberation.
World-Honored One!
We do not emerge from the various fetters. Why is this?
"World-Honored One, because this is the true limit (bhūtakoṭi) and is free from the characteristics of entanglement,
we do not seek to sever remorse."
Why is this? Because one who does not regret the True Dharma is called a śramaṇa,
World-Honored One!
We do not abandon or depart from doubt. Why is this?
Because we always have faith in the Dharma of pure liberation.
World-Honored One!
We do not extract the arrow of sorrow. Why is this?
Because we are permeated by faith in liberation,
World-Honored One,
we do not seek nirvana for ourselves.
"Why is this? Because all dharmas are ultimately *nirvāṇa*.
When this Dharma was being taught, two hundred bhikṣus attained liberation of mind through the non-arising of outflows (*āsrava*).

At that time, there were two hundred bhikṣus among the assembly who had previously attained the four dhyānas but harbored overweening pride; claiming they were in their final existence, they looked down upon others, rose from their seats and departed, saying:
"This Dharma that has been taught is in contradiction with all the world."
"We originally heard the teaching of the Dharma that is in accordance with truth, but now we hear what is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the word of the Teacher.
Pūrṇa said: "At that time, I immediately spoke to Mañjuśrī:"
These two hundred bhikṣus rose from their seats and departed, saying:
"The Dharma thus taught is in contradiction with all the world."
Mañjuśrī said: "Venerable Pūrṇa!
Because there are causes and conditions, this Dharma that has been taught is contrary to worldly conventions."
Why is this? Pūrṇa!

Those people in the world who dwell with attachment to the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense bases (āyatanas) desire to abandon birth and death and proceed toward nirvāṇa; yet they do not know that the true nature of birth and death is eternally unobtainable and is itself nirvāṇa. They do not know that within this there is no activity of birth and death, nor any arrival at nirvāṇa.
Patience is non-knowing; it is said to be contrary to the world of birth and death.
Those who calculate that there are four truths are in contradiction with this; within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), these four do not exist, nor is there a path or virtue.
As for "contradiction," it arises because one abides in duality; if one already abides in duality, there is contradiction.
Because the Path is equal, all phenomena are called non-dual; if one understands non-duality, then there is no contradiction.
If one calculates in terms of a self, there is overweening pride (*adhimāna*); where there is overweening pride, there is contradiction.

If one neither acts superiorly nor acts inferiorly, then within this equanimity, one does not act superiorly or inferiorly; there is neither action nor non-action. One who is thus is said to be without overweening pride; if there is no overweening pride, then there is no contradiction.
As the Buddha has said: "I do not dispute with the world; it is the world that disputes with me.
Why is this? Because the Buddha has completely severed all matters of contention and litigation.
What is the root of dispute?
It is that which is called "this is real" and "this is unreal," or "this is correct" and "this is erroneous.
As the Buddha has said regarding what a Brahmin calls "real": [it is that which accords with the Dharma].
What do you think? Is this false and not real?
Is it correct or erroneous?
"If both are non-existent, by what means do you know this?
At that time, Mañjuśrī manifested a vast conflagration before the path where the two hundred bhikṣus were traveling, making it impossible for them to pass.

In whichever direction they turned, they saw it filled with fire and were unable to pass through; they then attempted to ascend into the air by means of their supernormal powers, but above them they saw an iron net that hemmed them in and blocked their way.

At that time, the bhikṣu saw an iron net above and a great fire below; not knowing where he was, he was struck with terror and his hair stood on end. He saw only the path leading toward the Jeta Grove, adorned with various lotus flowers, and he saw a great multitude proceeding toward the Buddha, desiring to hear and receive the Dharma. He immediately turned back and went to the Kāliṅgara Flower Garden in the Jeta Grove to the place of the World-Honored One. Having arrived, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
Pūrṇa said: "At that time, I immediately asked those bhikṣus:
'Where have you gone?'"
"From where have you come?
The bhikṣus said, "Venerable Pūrṇa!"
"I am an arhat whose outflows are exhausted; I have attained the four dhyānas and possess all supernormal powers.
Having heard from the youth Mañjuśrī teachings that contradict the Dharma, I abandoned them and departed."

Seeing this buddha-field filled with a great conflagration that he could not cross, he immediately ascended into the void by means of his supernormal power; yet he saw an iron net covering him from above, while below him was the great fire.
"We now wish to ask the Buddha about the stage of an Arhat who has exhausted all outflows.
At that time, the Buddha said to me: "Pūrṇa!
If there were a great fire, it would be impossible for one to avoid that great fire. Pūrṇa!
If one has fallen into the net of views, it would be impossible for one to escape that iron net.
Pūrṇa! It is impossible for one who has fallen into the waters of craving to cross over the realm of water. Why is this?
Pūrṇa! These bhikṣus have not yet extinguished the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion; for this reason, they are unable to emerge from the fire. Pūrṇa!
These bhikṣus have fallen into the net of views; therefore, they cannot escape from the iron net. Pūrṇa!
These bhikṣus have fallen into the waters of craving; it is impossible for them to cross over the great flood.

Pūrṇa! This fire element, the iron net, and the water element have no place from which they come and no destination to which they go; it is through the power sustained by Mañjuśrī that such things are seen.

Pūrṇa! Greed, hatred, delusion, various views, existence, craving, and all such phenomena have no place from which they come and no destination to which they go. They arise from inverted thoughts, false imaginings, and the discrimination between self and others regarding desire and greed; therefore, birth and death are without self and belong to nothing.

If one gives rise to right practice with an undisturbed mind, adorning oneself with meditation in a secluded place, and having attained meditative absorption, neither giving rise to arrogance nor dwelling in or clinging to it, then with a concentrated mind one should observe all phenomena: what dharma is the cause?
"What phenomena are conditions?

Observing in this way and seeing according to reality, one sees that it is as follows: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise, and so on, up to the arising of this entire mass of suffering, including grief and lamentation; this is called falling into error."

Thus, with the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*), volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) cease, and so on, until the entire mass of suffering, including grief and lamentation, ceases; this is called right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).

This is the unconditioned state of correctness (*asaṃskṛta-samyaktva*): there is no past ignorance to be ceased, nor is there any future or present ignorance to be ceased; rather, it is simply through improper reflection that ignorance arises.
If ignorance ceases, improper mental attention no longer arises;
if improper mental attention ceases, ignorance also ceases.
When ignorance ceases, it is called ultimate cessation; therefore, with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease.

If one correctly contemplates and observes with wisdom as it truly is, this body composed of the four great elements is deluded and devoid of cognition; it is like grass, wood, tiles, or pebbles, like a shadow, or like a flame. As I have taught: "This body is thus, this mind is thus, this intellect is thus, and this consciousness is thus."
This mind has no form or color and cannot be grasped; it is like an illusion, ineffable, and cannot be found as being external, internal, or in between the two.
If there is a bhikṣu who thus accomplishes right reflection, he knows that all dharmas are originally unarisen; if a dharma is unarisen, it is the ultimate truth.
When this Dharma was being taught, these two hundred bhikṣus were no longer attached to any phenomena; their outflows were forever exhausted, and their minds attained liberation.

At that time, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son, having lost his followers, came to Śrāvastī in sorrow and displeasure. He went to the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, to where the World-Honored Buddha was staying in the Kāliṅga Garden. After exchanging greetings, he stood to one side and said: “Gautama!
"I have heard many times that the śramaṇa Gautama uses the power of illusory arts to seize the followers of others; today I see it with my own eyes.

He has caused Mañjuśrī to break up my assembly, leading them to the presence of the Buddha to practice false teachings. They do not come to me nor accept my instructions, but instead listen and act according to their own whims."
At that time, there was a renunciant non-Buddhist named Jayamati sitting in the assembly.
With a friendly and affectionate intent, this non-Buddhist Jayamati said to Saccaka:
"Stop, stop, Nirgrantha!

Do not harbor a disrespectful mind toward the World-Honored One, the community of bhikṣus, or Mañjuśrī; do not suffer loss for a long night or endure pain by falling into the evil realms, which are devoid of joy.
Satyaka Nirgrantha!
Listen as I speak a parable to clarify this meaning.

Suppose there were a person, foolish and lacking wisdom, who desired to seek out ghee; he took a vessel and went to the Ganges to fetch water, but having reached another place, he used a drill to churn it, undergoing great exhaustion and suffering, yet never seeing any ghee.
"Thus it is, Nigaṇṭha!

You followers of external paths who wish to cultivate the severing of fetters, receive precepts, and practice self-mortification—your modes of conduct and ritual applications are entirely erroneous and incapable of severing anything;
you are just like those people who take water from the Ganges."
Furthermore, if one gives rise to anger toward the Dharma of the World-Honored One’s taming, one shall fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts.
He spoke again:
“Nirgrantha!

Furthermore, there was another person who was intelligent from birth; when he wished to obtain fresh butter (*navanīta*), he took pure, high-quality milk and placed it in a vessel, churning it with a churning-stick. With very little effort, he obtained a great amount of fresh butter. From the fresh butter, he further obtained clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and from the clarified butter, he subsequently obtained the finest essence, *maṇḍa*.
"Thus it is, Nigaṇṭha!

Within the True Dharma of the Buddha, whether lay or ordained, those who possess complete pure faith and have much understanding and inclination, diligently practicing for superior progress, will swiftly attain liberation."
Just as that wise person, for the sake of obtaining ghee, places milk in a vessel.
Furthermore, Nigaṇṭha!
It is like two men, one of whom breaks another’s hundred thousand clay vessels and compensates him with fine jeweled vessels.
"Nirgrantha!
What do you think?
Would such a person be harming that other person?"
The Nirgrantha replied, “No, Jitaśatru!”
"Thus it is, Nigaṇṭha!
A disciple of an external path is like that earthen vessel; once broken, he enters the Dharma of the Tathāgata, just as one who obtains a precious vessel gains increase without any loss."
Furthermore, Nigaṇṭha!
Suppose there is a caravan leader who is foolish and lacks skillful means, leading a multitude of people onto a wrong path.
Then suppose there is another caravan leader possessed of great wisdom, who out of compassion for these people establishes them upon the correct path.
"Thus it is, Nigaṇṭhas!

Just as you claim to be teachers yourselves, you are those who do not know the path, who are not skilled in the path, who have not seen the path, and who cannot explain the path; therefore, you lead sentient beings toward what is not the path."

Now, the World-Honored One is a great caravan leader; he knows and guides the good path, seeing the path and proclaiming the path, leading all those of external paths and establishing them upon the correct road.
Nigaṇṭha!
"All of your followers are here; you may take them with you.
At that time, there were twelve thousand others who returned from Saccaka, having been converted to the Way.
As for the rest who remained and had already attained clear insight, the Buddha addressed them, saying:
"Welcome, bhikṣus!
and they all became śramaṇas.
At that time, the Buddha said to the non-Buddhist Jñānagupta:
"Do you see these twelve thousand people who are following after Satyaka?
"I see them," he replied.
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said: “Jayaśrī!
All these people shall surely be among the number of those in Maitreya Buddha’s first assembly. Why is this?
Because they have heard such profound Dharma and have made offerings to me.
Moreover, this Satyaka was foremost in wisdom among the disciples of Maitreya Buddha, just as Śāriputra is now foremost among my disciples. Why is this?
I know that this man has faith and understanding in me, yet because of his own conceit, he does not relinquish this view.
At that time, Jyotirasa said to Mañjuśrī, “In the future,
at the end of the age, will there be many bhikṣus who give rise to overweening pride?
Mañjuśrī replied:
“Good son! In the future final age, when the Dharma is about to perish, those who possess overweening pride will be exceedingly difficult to find. Why is this?
Because they are unable to practice and attain the four dhyānas, they give rise to overweening pride after having [supposedly] attained them.
Later, in the final age when the Dharma is about to perish, even the bhikṣus will be unable to settle their minds, let alone attain the four dhyānas.
Therefore, good son!
In the future final age, those who possess overweening pride will be exceedingly difficult to find.
Furthermore, good son!
There are two kinds of those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*). What are the two?
First, pride in views based on faith; second, pride regarding meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Those who give rise to pride regarding meditative absorption do so out of a desire for gain and fame;
such individuals of faith and view give rise to overweening pride and slander the Buddha’s true Dharma.
"Such persons of overweening pride shall fall into the hells, the animal realm,
or the realm of hungry ghosts. Viśeṣamati asked, "Mañjuśrī!"
"If one wishes to know that another's mind is characterized by overweening pride (*adhimāna*),
how should one know it? Mañjuśrī replied,
"An ordinary person who desires to attain *nirvāṇa* is, in reality, not an Arhat."
If, upon hearing this teaching, one is startled, terrified, or fearful, you should know that this is merely an ordinary person of overweening pride (adhimāna), and not a true Arhat of the Tathāgata.

If one hears from another and feels startled, fearful, or terrified, you should know that such a person is merely an ordinary worldling (*pṛthagjana*), one of overweening pride (*adhimāna*) and not an Arhat; though they may still be able to purely repay the kindness of those who bestow gifts upon them, they are nonetheless not an Arhat.
If one is free from all fetters and afflictions, they have no basis for attachment and are a field of merit for the world;
if one possesses all fetters and afflictions, they have a basis for attachment and are not a field of merit for the world.
If one dwells within this [state], know that such a person is characterized by overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
All phenomena are subsumed within *nirvāṇa*; if one discriminates and observes within this [state], know that such a person is characterized by overweening pride.
All dharmas should not be known, nor should they be abandoned; they should not be realized, nor should they be cultivated.
One who does not know this reality should be known as a person of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Jayaśrī asked: "Mañjuśrī!
What are the marks and signs of one who is free from overweening pride?"
Mañjuśrī said: “To not contradict non-extinction is the seal-mark of being free from overweening pride. Why is this?
There is no sound capable of causing that person to give rise to alarm, fear, or dread, just as no sound whatsoever can cause the lion king to be startled, terrified, or afraid.
It is the same for a bhikṣu free from overweening pride (*adhimāna*): upon hearing various sounds, he does not give rise to fear. Why is this?
Because he knows that sounds are like echoes; just as those echoing sounds possess no mind, intellect, or consciousness, yet still produce sound.
Thus, one knows the mind, intellect, and consciousness as they truly are: all sounds arise from conditions and possess no reality.
Having known this, one does not know what dharma could be definitively named "sound."

If one hears the voice of a Buddha and does not crave it, hears the voices of non-Buddhists and does not disparage them, hears the pure and wholesome Dharma and does not crave it, and hears defiled dharmas and does not disparage them, it is because they thoroughly understand the prior and posterior limits of all sounds.

These seals are free from overweening pride; they are the seal of neither high nor low, the seal of reality as it is, the seal of the path of right view, the seal of entering the single path, the seal of entering the equality of the dharma-realm, the seal of being without conceit, the seal of not contradicting suchness, the seal of abiding in the limit of reality, the seal of the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the seal of the equality of the three periods of time, the seal of primordial non-arising, and the seal of contemplating the true nature of all phenomena. Seals such as these seal all dharmas.

Such a bhikṣu is called one who is free from contention; having heard this, he has no doubt, is not startled, not terrified, not alarmed, and not afraid; he perceives neither a self nor dharmas, for all things are equal.
At that time, the non-Buddhist ascetic Jyotiska addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I have now, from this spiritual friend, heard of this true path and the merits of the Mahāyāna."
“World-Honored One!
Having now heard this Dharma taught by Mañjuśrī, I have resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Excellent, World-Honored One!”

I only pray that the Tathāgata will preach the Dharma as is appropriate, so that having heard it, I may swiftly cultivate and gather the factors conducive to enlightenment, and attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path for the sake of all immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings.
The Buddha told Jyotiṣmān:
"A bodhisattva has two dharmas by which they quickly attain clear penetration and become fully endowed with the Mahāyāna.
What are these two?"
These are what are called diligence and heedfulness.
Among these, diligence means relinquishing all wealth acquired in accordance with the Dharma;
heedfulness means giving without expecting recompense, dedicating it all toward omniscience.
Furthermore, diligence consists in correctly abandoning all evil and unwholesome dharmas and bringing all wholesome dharmas to full completion;
heedfulness consists in firmly upholding the pure precepts not for the sake of future rebirths, but dedicating them entirely toward the unsurpassed path.
Furthermore, one who is diligent practices patience without sparing even their own body or life;
one who is heedful harbors no intent to harm any sentient being.
Moreover, one who is diligent advances in all wholesome dharmas without weariness or fatigue.
One who is heedful advances all roots of goodness toward the unsurpassed path.
Furthermore, one who is diligent has no weariness of mind regarding the factors of dhyāna;
one who is heedful does not crave or become attached to the flavors of those factors of dhyāna.
Furthermore, one who is diligent advances toward extensive learning without ever feeling weary or satisfied;
one who is heedful practices with right mindfulness the noble knowledge and noble wisdom.
Furthermore, one who is diligent does not abandon the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).
One who is heedful gives rise to the transformation of sentient beings.
Furthermore, one who is diligent maintains firm stability of body and mind;
one who is heedful does not allow body and mind to abandon or become attached to dharmas.
Furthermore, one who is diligent takes all sentient beings as objects of focus with a mind of loving-kindness;
one who is heedful does not fail to attain the dharma of loving-kindness toward those sentient beings who are the objects of focus.
Furthermore, one who is diligent teaches other sentient beings to give rise to the mind of omniscience.
One who is heedful contemplates all phenomena as being entirely like illusions, yet does not abandon the mind of omniscience.
Furthermore, one who is diligent gives rise to samādhi;
one who is heedful protects it so that it does not fall into the exhaustion of outflows.
Furthermore, one who is diligent cultivates and accumulates the Noble Truths as if their head were on fire;
one who is heedful does not follow after the realization of cessation.
Furthermore, one who is diligent tirelessly accumulates wholesome qualities in order to fulfill all the marks [of a Buddha].
The heedful one contemplates the Dharma-body;
furthermore, the diligent one cultivates the purification of Buddha-lands,
while the heedful one purifies the realm of sentient beings.
Furthermore, one who is diligent accumulates the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment;
one who is heedful dwells securely in the dharma of tranquil liberation.
You should know this, Victorious Will!
All the skillful means and karmic activities of a bodhisattva are accomplished through diligence;
all the activities of omniscience of a bodhisattva are achieved by means of heedfulness.
Therefore it is said: "The Bodhisattva who has accomplished wisdom and skillful means does not fear falling back from the unsurpassed right path.

When this Dharma was being taught, the non-Buddhist practitioner Jyotiṣka attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas; his mind was pure and filled with joy, and he ascended into the air to a height of seven tala trees.
The trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and a great light shone everywhere.
The musical instruments of the devas resounded spontaneously without being struck, and the heavens rained down a profusion of flowers.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the resolve of Vijaya, smiled. It is the constant law of all Buddhas that when they smile, hundreds of thousands of multicolored rays of light issue from the gateway of their mouth, universally illuminating immeasurable and boundless worlds. They pass upward beyond the Brahma-world, eclipsing the light of the sun and moon and obscuring the palaces of Māra; then, having circled the body to the right hundreds of thousands of times, they re-enter through the crown of the head.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, rose from his seat, adjusted his robes so as to bare his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee upon the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
“Flowers of wisdom and the power of merit, A halo that guides the world;
Flowers of the thirty-two marks, Adorned with various secondary characteristics.”
Your conduct is like that of an elephant or a lion; with the courageous power of diligence, you have emerged.
For what reason, World-Honored One, do you smile?
We pray that the Guide will explain it to us.
His speech is like the sound of thunder;
the Buddha’s voice is a lion’s roar, the call of the kalaviṅka bird, and a soft, pure brahma-sound.
It pervades the sounds of the three-thousandfold world system, reaching both devas and humans.
If one wishes to compare it to the Buddha’s voice, no calculation can reach it.
The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, as well as all the Bodhisattvas—though their wisdom is peerless, none is equal to the Buddha; they do not know the All-Knowledge.
The Muni, with his power of wisdom, has declared: for what reason do you smile?
If humans, devas, nāgas, and asuras hear it, they shall swiftly attain bodhi.
Their minds will be freed from the two extremes, nor will they cling to the middle.
All things are without attachment, equal to empty space;
all things are beyond counting, transcending the entire world.
I ask you, whose wisdom is equal to space: for what cause and condition do you smile?
Blue, green, golden, crimson, purple, red, and white light—
flames emerging from the gateway of the face— as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
universally illumine immeasurable realms, vast and far-reaching like space.
The evil realms are extinguished and happiness is attained because the light of the Guide has touched them.
If light is emitted from his knees, this is the bestowal of a prediction for a śrāvaka;
if light is emitted from his hands, this is the prediction for a pratyekabuddha.
The Buddha definitively proclaims the Mahāyāna, the path of all-encompassing wisdom;
having brought light and benefit to sentient beings, he returns to the stainless crown.
Excellent, O God among Men, the Sage honored by the three realms!
We pray that you will explain this according to reality; O Guide, speak with single-minded resolve.
To sever our doubts and gladden the great assembly, for what cause and condition do you smile?
When hundreds of thousands of millions of sentient beings have heard it, their hearts will be filled with joy.
Having been thus requested, the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Do you see this good man, Viśeṣamati?

He has ascended into the air to the height of seven tala trees, attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), joined his palms to pay homage to me, and is being honored by hundreds of thousands of devas."
Ānanda replied,
“I have seen them,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said, “Ānanda!

This good man Jyotiṣka has, in the presence of seventy-two billion Buddhas, planted various roots of goodness and practiced the bodhisattva path, cultivating and accumulating the unsurpassed, right, and true Way.”

At that time, he constantly became a great universal monarch (cakravartin), reverently making offerings to these Tathāgatas, honoring and praising them, always practicing the pure life (brahmacarya), and fully upholding and protecting the teachings of all these Buddhas.

Ānanda! From this day forward, this good man Jetaśaya shall encounter immeasurable and incalculable Buddhas, honoring, making offerings to, respecting, and praising them; he shall constantly practice the holy life and cause immeasurable asaṃkhyeya sentient beings to abide in the path to Bodhi.

After having accumulated the path to enlightenment for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas beyond this, he shall attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path and become a most perfectly awakened one, appearing in the world as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and so forth, up to Buddha, World-Honored One, named Jñānaprabharāja.
The land is named Delightful Vision, and the eon is named Adorned with a Single Jewel. Ānanda!
The objects of enjoyment in that land of Delightful Vision are like those in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations.

The sentient beings of that land do not leak [sensations] regarding form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or mental phenomena, and they are free from all unwholesome forms. Those sentient beings respect one another with joy and delight; all of them go to see the Buddha King of Wisdom-Light, and even in their dreams they constantly see the Buddha, never being separated from mindfulness of the Buddha. For this reason, that land is named "Delightful Vision."

In this kalpa, only one Tathāgata performs the Buddha-work; the lifespan of both the Buddha and the sentient beings is equal to one kalpa. For this reason, that kalpa is named "Adorned with a Single Jewel."
Ānanda! This Buddha King Jñānaprabha has a community of bodhisattvas numbering nine hundred and twenty billion, all of whom attained the stage of non-retrogression at his first assembly.

When this Tathāgata King Jñānaprabha is about to enter parinirvāṇa, he will first bestow the prediction of enlightenment upon the bodhisattva Siṃhagati, saying: "You shall become a buddha named Siṃhākāra Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha... [down to] Buddha, World-Honored One. His lifespan shall be ten intermediate kalpas, after which he will enter parinirvāṇa; there shall then be an immeasurable and boundless community of bodhisattvas.

At the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, a single stūpa was erected for his entire body-relics, measuring sixty yojanas in length and breadth and eighty yojanas in height; it was adorned with various jewels, and immeasurable sentient beings made offerings to it.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Jyotirasa descended from the sky, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and addressed the Buddha with verses on the indestructible Dharma-realm:
“The realm of form and the Dharma-realm, The realm of sentient beings—all are equal.
This realm is equal to the realm of wisdom; Now you have bestowed upon me my prediction.”
The realm of sensation and the realm of afflictions are equal to the realm of space;
all phenomena are likewise this realm, and now I have come in accordance with it.
The realm of phenomena, the realm of desire, and the three realms as well—[all are thus].
Equal to empty space, I declare them to be just so.
The realm of birth and death and nirvana abide equally within the Dharma-realm;
this element and the water element, the earth element and the fire and wind elements—[are all likewise].
The aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus)— the eye-element and the eye-consciousness-element,
the mind-element and the mental-object-element— these objective spheres are equal.
You have not granted me a prediction regarding the aggregates, nor have you granted me a prediction regarding the elements or the bases.
He does not grant a prediction regarding name-and-form, nor does he grant a prediction regarding the internal or external;
for one knows by means of sound.
Sound itself is quiescent, and the Buddha has no mind or will.
Forming this thought, I receive the prediction: "I too am without consciousness;
having received the prediction of the Way, as I am, so is the Buddha;
as the Buddha is, so am I; and so it is for all sentient beings."
Thus they receive their prediction;
as they completely relinquish all things, they do not disrupt the dharma-realm and abide securely in the limit of reality.
"Entering equally into all phenomena, like space which is without action,
because of having learned and known skillful means. At that time,
after the Bodhisattva Viśeṣamati had praised the Buddha with these verses, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and withdrew to sit on one side.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"Receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, and widely expound this sutra for others among the great assembly.
Ānanda replied:
"I have received and upheld it,
World-Honored One!
What is the name of this sutra?"
"How should this be received and upheld? The Buddha told Ānanda:

"This sutra is named 'Sustained by the Supernatural Powers of Mañjuśrī'; it is also named 'Eliminating the Sounds of All Māras and Heretics'; it is also named 'Gathering Jewels'; and it is also named 'The Jewel Casket. It should be received and upheld in this way."

When this sutra had been spoken, the youth Mañjuśrī, the bodhisattva Jayamati, and others, as well as the great śrāvaka, the venerable Ānanda, and the entire great assembly—including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gods, humans, gandharvas, and so forth—having heard what the Buddha had taught, were all greatly filled with joy.
The Mahāvaipulya Ratnakaraṇḍa Sūtra, Scroll II.
